The evaluation provides only a limited comparison of model performance. With two forecast years, individual errors have a large influence on the accuracy measures. A model that performs well for these observations may behave differently over a longer period.

The naïve model achieved the lowest RMSE and MAE, indicating that using the latest observed GPU demand produced smaller errors than extending a trend during this short evaluation. However, this result does not establish that GPU demand will remain constant or that the naïve method is suitable for forecasting through 2030.

@tbl-gpu-accuracy reports the calculated accuracy results for the four models.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gpu-accuracy
#| tbl-cap: "Exploratory rolling-origin forecast accuracy for GPU demand, 2025–2026."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

gpu_accuracy <- gpu_cv_long |>
  dplyr::group_by(model) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    RMSE = sqrt(
      mean((actual - forecast)^2)
    ),
    MAE = mean(
      abs(actual - forecast)
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(RMSE) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    `RMSE rank` = dplyr::row_number()
  )

gpu_accuracy_table <- gpu_accuracy |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Model = as.character(model),
    `RMSE (million GPU-hours)` = round(RMSE, 3),
    `MAE (million GPU-hours)` = round(MAE, 3),
    `RMSE rank` = `RMSE rank`
  )

knitr::kable(
  gpu_accuracy_table,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r")
)
```

The naïve benchmark achieved the lowest RMSE (0.441 million GPU-hours) and MAE (0.353 million GPU-hours), followed by drift, log-linear trend and linear trend. Unlike the overall HPC and CPU evaluations, the simpler benchmark performed better than the models estimating historical growth.

Figure 7 shows that all four models underestimated GPU demand in 2026. The naïve model projected approximately 2.39 million GPU-hours, compared with the estimated value of 3.00 million GPU-hours. The trend models also failed to anticipate this increase. This illustrates the difficulty of forecasting GPU demand when the historical series contains substantial changes over a short period.

The accuracy rankings should nevertheless be interpreted cautiously. Only two forecast errors were available for each model, and the underlying GPU-hour series includes derived estimates and conversion assumptions. Consequently, the evaluation does not provide sufficient evidence to establish that the naïve model will remain the most accurate approach over a longer forecast horizon.

The naïve model was retained as a reference because of its lower evaluation errors. Linear and log-linear models were also retained to examine the consequences of different growth assumptions. However, none of these models was selected as a reliable central GPU forecast.

Following the project review, GPU projections were treated as exploratory and excluded from the initial national HPC planning scenarios. Those scenarios instead use the selected overall HPC demand projection and historical Field of Research allocation shares. This distinction prevents the more uncertain GPU estimates from being presented as independently validated planning requirements.

The exploratory GPU projections are presented in Section 4.3 to show how different modelling assumptions affect the results through 2030. More consistent historical records of GPU requests, allocations and usage, together with validated conversion factors, would be needed to support reliable GPU-specific forecasting.


### Residual Diagnostics

The rolling-origin evaluation assessed how accurately the forecasting models predicted observations excluded from their training samples. Residual diagnostics were then conducted on the selected linear trend models for overall HPC and CPU demand, using the complete 2014–2026 historical series.

The purpose was to examine whether the fitted models left systematic patterns in their errors and whether their residual distributions supported the assumptions used to construct statistical prediction intervals.

Residual autocorrelation was examined using the autocorrelation function (ACF) and the Ljung–Box test. Normal Q–Q plots were also examined to assess departures from the normal-error assumption. These diagnostics complement the out-of-sample evaluation presented in Sections 4.2.1 and 4.2.2.

Figure @fig-model-diagnostics presents the residual diagnostics for both selected models.

```{r}
#| label: fig-model-diagnostics
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics for the selected linear trend models fitted to 2014–2026: residual ACF and normal Q–Q plots for overall HPC and CPU demand."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| out-width: 100%
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)

# Prepare the historical series used for forecasting
hpc_diagnostic_data <- annual_analysis |>
  transmute(
    year = as.integer(year),
    demand = as.numeric(demand_ksu)
  ) |>
  arrange(year)

cpu_diagnostic_data <- annual_converted |>
  transmute(
    year = as.integer(year),
    demand = as.numeric(demand_cpu_core_hours) / 1e6
  ) |>
  arrange(year)

stopifnot(
  identical(hpc_diagnostic_data$year, 2014:2026),
  identical(cpu_diagnostic_data$year, 2014:2026),
  all(is.finite(hpc_diagnostic_data$demand)),
  all(is.finite(cpu_diagnostic_data$demand))
)

# Fit selected linear trend models using all 13 observations
hpc_diagnostic_fit <- lm(
  demand ~ year,
  data = hpc_diagnostic_data
)

cpu_diagnostic_fit <- lm(
  demand ~ year,
  data = cpu_diagnostic_data
)

# Function for residual ACF plots
make_acf_plot <- function(model, title) {

  residual_values <- residuals(model)

  acf_result <- acf(
    residual_values,
    plot = FALSE,
    lag.max = 5
  )

  acf_data <- tibble(
    lag = as.numeric(acf_result$lag)[-1],
    autocorrelation = as.numeric(acf_result$acf)[-1]
  )

  # Approximate reference limits, not a formal
  # hypothesis test for individual residual lags
  confidence_limit <- 1.96 / sqrt(length(residual_values))

  ggplot(
    acf_data,
    aes(
      x = lag,
      y = autocorrelation
    )
  ) +
    geom_hline(
      yintercept = 0,
      colour = "#555555"
    ) +
    geom_hline(
      yintercept = c(
        -confidence_limit,
        confidence_limit
      ),
      colour = "#CC6677",
      linetype = "dashed",
      linewidth = 0.6
    ) +
    geom_segment(
      aes(
        xend = lag,
        yend = 0
      ),
      colour = "#0077A8",
      linewidth = 1
    ) +
    geom_point(
      colour = "#0077A8",
      size = 2
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(
      breaks = 1:5
    ) +
    coord_cartesian(
      ylim = c(-1, 1)
    ) +
    labs(
      title = title,
      x = "Lag (years)",
      y = "Residual ACF"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
}

# Function for normal Q-Q plots
make_qq_plot <- function(model, title) {

  residual_data <- tibble(
    residual = as.numeric(residuals(model))
  )

  ggplot(
    residual_data,
    aes(sample = residual)
  ) +
    stat_qq(
      colour = "#0077A8",
      size = 2
    ) +
    stat_qq_line(
      colour = "#CC6677",
      linewidth = 0.8
    ) +
    labs(
      title = title,
      x = "Theoretical quantiles",
      y = "Residual quantiles"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
}

# Create four diagnostic panels
p_hpc_acf <- make_acf_plot(
  hpc_diagnostic_fit,
  "A. HPC residual ACF"
)

p_hpc_qq <- make_qq_plot(
  hpc_diagnostic_fit,
  "B. HPC normal Q-Q plot"
)

p_cpu_acf <- make_acf_plot(
  cpu_diagnostic_fit,
  "C. CPU residual ACF"
)

p_cpu_qq <- make_qq_plot(
  cpu_diagnostic_fit,
  "D. CPU normal Q-Q plot"
)

(p_hpc_acf | p_hpc_qq) /
  (p_cpu_acf | p_cpu_qq) +
  plot_annotation(
    caption = paste(
      "Diagnostics use in-sample residuals from",
      "linear trend models fitted to 2014–2026.",
      "Dashed ACF lines are approximate reference limits.",
      "CPU residuals are measured in million core-hours."
    )
  )
```

The residual ACF plots show relatively small correlations for both models. None of the displayed correlations exceeds the approximate reference limits.

For overall HPC demand, the residual correlations are close to zero across most displayed lags. This suggests that the linear trend captures much of the systematic movement in the historical series, although the short sample limits the strength of this conclusion.

CPU residuals show a more noticeable negative correlation at lag 1 and lag 4. These correlations remain within the approximate reference limits, but they indicate that some year-to-year variation may not be fully captured by a single linear trend.

The Ljung–Box test was used to examine whether the residual autocorrelations were jointly distinguishable from zero over the first three lags. Table @tbl-ljung-box reports the results.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ljung-box
#| tbl-cap: "Ljung–Box tests of residual autocorrelation for the selected linear trend models, using three lags."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

diagnostic_lag <- 3

# No ARMA error terms were fitted.
# fitdf = 0 retains the three test degrees of freedom.
hpc_lb <- Box.test(
  residuals(hpc_diagnostic_fit),
  lag = diagnostic_lag,
  type = "Ljung-Box",
  fitdf = 0
)

cpu_lb <- Box.test(
  residuals(cpu_diagnostic_fit),
  lag = diagnostic_lag,
  type = "Ljung-Box",
  fitdf = 0
)

diagnostic_results <- tibble(
  `Demand measure` = c(
    "Overall HPC",
    "CPU"
  ),
  `Ljung-Box statistic` = c(
    unname(hpc_lb$statistic),
    unname(cpu_lb$statistic)
  ),
  `Lag` = diagnostic_lag,
  `Degrees of freedom` = c(
    unname(hpc_lb$parameter),
    unname(cpu_lb$parameter)
  ),
  `p-value` = c(
    hpc_lb$p.value,
    cpu_lb$p.value
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    `Ljung-Box statistic` = round(
      `Ljung-Box statistic`, 3
    ),
    `p-value` = round(
      `p-value`, 3
    )
  )

knitr::kable(
  diagnostic_results,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r")
)
```

The Ljung–Box results do not provide sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis of no residual autocorrelation at the tested lags for either selected model, using a 5% significance level.

However, the results should not be interpreted as proof that the residuals are independent. Each model was fitted using only 13 annual observations, and the test has limited power with such a small sample. The ACF reference limits are also approximate.

The normal Q–Q plots provide additional information about the distribution of the fitted errors.

For overall HPC demand, most residuals lie reasonably close to the theoretical reference line, although some departures are visible around the centre and upper tail. The plot does not show an obvious severe departure from normality, but the small sample makes the distribution difficult to assess reliably.

The CPU Q–Q plot shows more noticeable departures, particularly in the lower tail. The most negative residual falls substantially below the reference line, suggesting that the normal-error assumption may be less suitable for CPU demand.

These differences matter when interpreting model-based prediction intervals. The intervals depend on assumptions about the fitted error distribution, and departures from those assumptions may affect their coverage. The CPU intervals therefore require particular caution.

Overall, the diagnostics do not reveal strong evidence of residual autocorrelation in the selected linear models. However, they do not establish that the fitted trends or their error distributions will remain unchanged through 2030.

The residual diagnostics support the use of the linear models as interpretable forecasting references, while reinforcing the need to consider alternative growth assumptions and sensitivity to the 2026 observation. These issues are examined in Section 4.3.

### Evaluation Summary

The model evaluation produced different results across the three computing measures.

For overall HPC demand, the linear trend achieved the lowest RMSE and MAE and was selected as the central forecasting model.

For CPU demand, the linear and log-linear trends performed similarly, but the linear model was preferred because it provided a simpler and more transparent basis for long-term projection.

For GPU demand, the naïve benchmark performed best over the two available evaluation years, although the limited sample prevented a reliable assessment of longer-term predictive performance.

The results demonstrate why model selection cannot depend solely on the lowest historical forecast error. The forecasting horizon, historical data coverage, measurement assumptions and sensitivity to recent observations also need to be considered.

The selected models and alternative growth assumptions form the basis for the demand projections and scenarios presented in the following section.

## Demand Forecasts to 2030

### Overall HPC Demand

The selected linear trend projects overall HPC demand of approximately 2.02 million kSU in 2027, increasing to 2.50 million kSU in 2030.

The model excluding the 2026 observation produces a lower 2030 projection of approximately 2.29 million kSU. In contrast, the log-linear model projects approximately 6.48 million kSU.

The difference illustrates the sensitivity of longer-term projections to the latest observation and the assumed growth pattern. The log-linear trajectory should not be interpreted as a validated upper bound because it performed less well during historical evaluation.

### CPU Demand

The central CPU forecast increases from approximately 1.13 billion core-hours in 2027 to 1.37 billion core-hours in 2030.

Excluding 2026 reduces the 2030 projection to approximately 1.26 billion core-hours, while the log-linear model produces approximately 2.48 billion core-hours.

The central linear model provides a reference for planning, while the alternative trajectories illustrate the consequences of different growth assumptions.

### GPU Demand

GPU projections show greater uncertainty because of the shorter historical series.

The naïve benchmark maintains the latest estimate at approximately 3.00 million GPU-hours through 2030. The linear trend projects approximately 3.37 million GPU-hours, while the log-linear trend projects approximately 3.68 million GPU-hours.

These are exploratory scenarios rather than reliable long-term predictions. The short historical record limits the ability to determine whether GPU demand will stabilise or continue growing.

## Field of Research Scenarios

The FoR scenarios apply alternative historical allocation compositions to the projected overall HPC demand.

Three reference periods were considered: the earlier period (2014–2020), the recent period (2021–2026) and the full period (2014–2026).

The recent-period composition gives greater weight to Engineering and Technology, while the earlier-period composition places greater emphasis on Earth and Environmental Sciences.

These differences affect the indicative distribution of future HPC resources across disciplines. However, the estimates are conditional on historical allocation shares and do not represent independently modelled FoR-specific demand.

The comparison is therefore more useful for examining the sensitivity of future resource distribution to allocation assumptions than for predicting precise disciplinary requirements.

## Summary of Results

The historical analysis identifies increasing pressure between recorded HPC demand and available allocations, particularly in 2026. CPU and GPU demand also show different measurement and forecasting challenges, with GPU analysis constrained by the shorter and less consistent historical record.

The linear trend provides the central forecast for overall HPC and CPU demand. By 2030, these models project approximately 2.50 million kSU and 1.37 billion CPU core-hours, respectively.

GPU forecasts remain exploratory, while FoR scenarios show how assumptions about historical allocation composition affect the indicative distribution of future resources.

These results provide the basis for the discussion of forecasting uncertainty and national HPC planning implications in the following chapter.


# Discussion

## Interpretation of the Main Findings

The historical records show a persistent difference between requested and allocated HPC resources. This difference was particularly pronounced in 2026. It indicates pressure within the reported allocation system, although it cannot be interpreted as a direct measure of all unmet research demand. Researchers may adjust requests to expected capacity, and some potential demand is not captured by the allocation process.

The forecast evaluation favoured a linear trend for overall HPC demand and CPU demand. These models produced competitive one-step-ahead accuracy and avoided the assumption that historical proportional growth would continue unchanged through 2030. Nevertheless, the central projections remain conditional on the historical accounting measures and the assumption that recent trends provide useful information about future requests.

The GPU results require greater caution. The model comparison used only two evaluation years, and the 2022–2026 modelling series includes derived estimates. Differences between the naïve, linear and log-linear projections should therefore be read as exploratory outcomes under different assumptions, not as evidence that one growth path will occur.

## Implications for National HPC Planning

The analysis provides a documented basis for discussing the scale and direction of reported HPC demand. The projected increase in overall requests suggests that national infrastructure planning should consider demand growth alongside the historical difference between requests and allocations.

However, forecast kSU values are accounting measures rather than direct measures of interchangeable computing capacity. Hardware changes, system-specific service-unit factors, GPU adoption and the design of allocation schemes may all affect the relationship between reported requests and the resources required to meet them.

The FoR scenarios provide a complementary view of possible distributional changes. They show that the implied allocation of future resources across disciplines depends on which historical period is used to represent research-field composition. These results are suitable for sensitivity analysis but should not be treated as direct forecasts of unmet demand within individual disciplines.

## Limitations and Future Work

The principal limitation is the short and uneven historical record. Overall HPC and CPU demand contain 13 annual observations, while the GPU modelling period contains only five. Historical differences in reporting scope and conversion assumptions also limit comparisons across facilities and years.

The analysis relies on publicly available records. It does not incorporate confidential application-level information, direct measures of rejected or discouraged requests, or future changes in policy and computing technology. Consequently, the forecasts should be updated as more consistent annual records become available.

Future work could improve the analysis by obtaining longer and more detailed requested-versus-allocated series, validating conversion factors directly with facility operators, and recording CPU and GPU demand using stable resource definitions. Consistent FoR-level request data would also allow research-field demand to be modelled directly rather than approximated through allocation shares.

# Conclusion

This project assembled and standardised publicly available Australian national research HPC records covering 2014–2026 and developed demand projections through 2030. It combined data preparation, conversion validation, descriptive analysis, rolling-origin forecast evaluation and scenario development.

The historical analysis found that recorded HPC requests exceeded allocations throughout the study period. For overall HPC demand and CPU demand, the linear trend was selected as the central forecasting approach. The corresponding 2030 projections were approximately 2.50 million kSU and 1.37 billion CPU core-hours. Alternative models produced substantially different outcomes, particularly under compounded proportional growth assumptions.

GPU forecasts and FoR scenarios were treated more cautiously because of limited historical coverage and the distinction between allocated resources and independently observed demand. The results offer a transparent reference for future infrastructure discussions rather than a precise estimate of unconstrained national computing requirements.

The main contribution is a reproducible analytical framework that makes the underlying data sources, conversion assumptions, model choices and forecasting limitations explicit. The accompanying technical Quarto documentation and Git repository preserve the detailed implementation for review and future updates.
